target.title: Modeling Coarticulation in EMG-based Continuous Speech Recognition

read.pdf: Fig. 1–9 captions/labels and Tables 1–4 as represented in text.txt; no separate PDF file was present.

entries.text: The EMG-PIT corpus contains 78 speakers, including 14 pilot-study speakers and 64 in the main collection; it includes audible and mouthed-silent speech.
entries.condition: Corpus overview; 14 pilot speakers and 64 main-collection speakers; both audible and silent/mouthed speech recorded.

entries.text: Pilot participants recorded two sessions each; the other participants recorded one session each. All participants were women aged 18–35 with normal vocal qualities.
entries.condition: Corpus demographics and session counts; participants recruited primarily from the University of Pittsburgh and Carnegie Mellon student populations.

entries.text: The corpus totals 92 sessions, with 4,600 audible and 4,600 silent utterances and 395 audible / 361 silent recording minutes.
entries.condition: EMG-PIT total across pilot and main collections, Table 1; values are corpus totals, not the experiment test-set size.

entries.text: Each session used 10 common BASE and 40 speaker-specific SPEC read sentences in each speaking mode; the 101-word vocabulary is the BASE vocabulary.
entries.unit: utterances per batch; words in BASE vocabulary
entries.condition: Controlled, phonetically balanced reading; BASE items are shared across speakers and SPEC items are speaker-specific; audible and silent parts each include a BASE and SPEC set.

entries.text: EMG was acquired with an 8-channel Varioport system at 600 Hz; five channels (1, 2, 3, 4, 6) were used, with the fifth physical channel reserved for other electrode-position experiments.
entries.condition: Varioport acquisition; amplification factor 1,170; 16-bit A/D conversion; 0.033 microvolts/bit; 0.9–295 Hz range; channels 1, 2, and 6 bipolar, channels 3, 4, and 5 unipolar; two mastoid references; channel 5 not used in this paper's experiments. Simultaneous acoustic audio was 16 kHz, 16-bit PCM.

entries.text: TD15 time-domain features were computed per EMG channel and stacked across the five channels; frame size was 27 ms and shift 10 ms, with a 15-frame stacking width.
entries.unit: ms frame size; ms frame shift; frames; input dimensions; LDA coefficients per frame
entries.condition: Baseline preprocessing; TD15 comprises time-domain mean, power, rectified-signal power and zero-crossing rate features; LDA reduces 775 dimensions to 32.

entries.text: Audible acoustic recordings were forced-aligned to initialize EMG phoneme models; the acoustic aligner was a Broadcast News recognizer.
entries.condition: Acoustic alignment used a JRTk HMM recognizer with quintphones, 6,000 distributions sharing 2,000 codebooks; its stated 10.2% WER was on the clean F0 official Broadcast News test set, not the EMG test set.

entries.text: The baseline is a context-independent phoneme HMM with 45 phoneme models plus silence, three left-to-right states per phoneme, Gaussian-mixture emissions and diagonal covariances.
entries.unit: phoneme models; states per phoneme; total models; total Gaussians
entries.condition: Speaker-dependent baseline; four Viterbi-training iterations; Gaussian count chosen by merge-and-split training on training data, averaging roughly two Gaussians per model.

entries.text: Decoding used a Broadcast News trigram LM, Viterbi decoding and lattice rescoring over word-penalty and LM-weight parameters.
entries.condition: The manuscript says the parameter matrix was used to obtain optimal recognition results; the LM training-data partition, parameter grid/ranges and final selected values are not given.
entries.quote: For decoding, we apply a trigram language model trained on Broadcast News data.

entries.text: The principal speaker-dependent evaluation used audible BASE test utterances and audible SPEC training utterances for the pilot speakers; no silent-speech recognition score is reported.
entries.unit: sessions; speakers; test utterances per speaker; BASE vocabulary words
entries.condition: Test set is 28 speaker-sessions from 14 pilot speakers, with 10 BASE utterances per speaker and 101-word BASE vocabulary; each speaker's SPEC batch supplies training data.
entries.quote:
We use
the batch of speaker-speciﬁc audible SPEC utterances as training set, and
the audible BASE utterances as testing set.

entries.text: The speaker-dependent phoneme baseline has average WER 47.15% on the audible BASE test condition.
entries.condition: 14 pilot speakers, 28 sessions, 10 audible BASE test utterances per speaker, 101-word vocabulary; audible SPEC training; Broadcast News trigram LM.
entries.quote: The average Word Error Rate obtained with this baseline speaker-dependent EMG-based recognition system is 47.15%.

entries.text: The Broadcast News trigram LM has test-set perplexity 24.24.
entries.condition: Speaker-dependent audible BASE test set; 14 pilot speakers, 28 sessions, 101-word vocabulary.

entries.text: Nine binary phonetic features with more than 50,000 training frames each were retained for PF experiments.
entries.condition: Selected from the available training data: Voiced, Consonant, Vowel, Alveolar, Unround, Fricative, Unvoiced, Front and Plosive.
entries.quote: To ensure reliable estimates for the PFs in our experiments, we limited ourselves to the nine phonetic features in the database which had more than 50000 frames of training data.

entries.text: The authors introduce data-driven bundling of interdependent phonetic features as a way to model coarticulation in EMG recognition.
entries.condition: Decision-tree clustering asks phonetic-feature questions; BDPF models bundle dependent features rather than treating each PF stream as statistically independent.
entries.quote: Accordingly, we call these models Bundled Phonetic Features (BDPF).

entries.text: PF bundling uses decision trees, with entropy-loss maximization over Gaussian-mixture weights as the split criterion and a fixed leaf-count stopping rule.
entries.unit: leaves per PF stream in speaker-dependent experiments
entries.condition: Separate trees for beginning, middle and end states and for present/absent feature models; nine PF streams; the leaf count was experimentally selected on the test set.
entries.quote:
Our termination criterion is that a ﬁxed number of 70 tree leaves for
each phonetic feature, corresponding to 70 independent models, is generated
for each PF stream.

entries.text: Because the available training set was small, the authors optimized PF-bundling parameters on the test set.
entries.condition: Speaker-dependent PF bundling; no independent validation set is described.
entries.quote: Note that due to the small number of training utterances, we optimized the parameters for the PF bundling on the test set.

entries.text: For context-independent PF decoding, test-set-selected weights were 0.04 for each PF stream and 0.64 for the phoneme stream.
entries.condition: Nine PF streams; weights were experimentally determined on the same test set used to report the speaker-dependent results.
entries.quote: the optimal PF stream weighting was experimentally determined on the test set to be 0.04 for each stream

entries.text: Adding context-independent PF streams changes average WER from 47.15% to 45.50%, an absolute reduction of 1.65 percentage points and a 3.5% relative improvement.
entries.unit: % WER; percentage-point absolute reduction; % relative improvement
entries.condition: 14 pilot speakers, 28 audible speaker-sessions, 10 BASE test utterances per speaker, 101-word vocabulary; PF weights selected on test set; trigram LM.
entries.quote:
The decrease from 47.15% to 45.50% WER corresponds to an absolute
system improvement of 1.65% WER and a relative improvement of 3.5%

entries.text: Context-independent PF versus phoneme-baseline comparison is reported significant by a paired-measures Student t-test at α = 0.7% (0.007).
entries.condition: Paired speaker-dependent comparison across the experiment's test measures; no confidence interval is reported.

entries.text: The authors say PF classifiers alone are not accurate enough to replace phoneme models; increasing their stream weight above 0.04 reduces performance.
entries.condition: Context-independent PF plus phoneme model experiments.

entries.text: The speaker-dependent bundled-PF system used equal PF weights of 0.11 for each of nine streams and a 0.01 phoneme-stream weight.
entries.condition: Nine context-independent BDPF feature streams; paper says these optimal weights were found experimentally, after test-set optimization of PF-bundling parameters.
entries.quote: the optimal weighting of the PF streams was 0.11 for each of the nine features, while the phoneme stream was factored in by a weight of only 0.01.

entries.text: Speaker-dependent context-independent bundled PFs achieve 35.78% average WER, a 24.1% relative reduction from the 47.15% phoneme baseline.
entries.condition: 14 pilot speakers and 28 sessions; audible BASE test / speaker-specific audible SPEC training; 101-word vocabulary; bundling has 70 leaves per PF stream and parameters were optimized on the test set.
entries.quote: PF clustering drastically reduces the WER to 35.78%, which is a relative improvement of 24.1% compared to the baseline system.

entries.text: Context-dependent unbundled PFs achieve 41.99% WER (described as about 42%), while context-independent bundled PFs achieve 35.78%.
entries.condition: Speaker-dependent audible BASE evaluation across 14 pilot speakers / 28 sessions; 101-word vocabulary; same reported baseline experiment.
entries.quote:
However, if we use context-
dependent unbundled PFs, the WER drastically increases to about 42%.

entries.text: Context-dependent bundled PFs achieve the best average speaker-dependent WER, 31.49%, a further 12% relative gain over the context-independent bundled-PF system.
entries.unit: % WER; % relative gain over 35.78% BDPF system
entries.condition: 14 pilot speakers / 28 sessions; audible BASE test and audible SPEC training; 101-word vocabulary; context-dependent BDPF streams; nine PF streams and 70 leaves per stream.
entries.quote: another 12% relative, giving the best average WER of 31.49% so far, again a statistically highly signiﬁcant improvement.

entries.text: The best speaker-dependent system is reported at about 10% WER for the best-performing speaker and 50% for the worst-performing speaker.
entries.condition: Context-dependent bundled PF system; speaker-dependent audible BASE test; 101-word vocabulary; the manuscript does not identify the speaker IDs in this sentence.

entries.text: Table 3 reports sequential relative gains of 3.5%, 7.7%, 14.8% and 12.0% for CI PF, CD PF, bundled PF and CD bundled PF steps, respectively; all are marked significant.
entries.unit: % relative gain at each successive comparison
entries.condition: Speaker-dependent average WER table; gains compare each row with the immediately preceding system (the manuscript also separately reports 24.1% bundled-PF gain versus the phoneme baseline). Significance marker *; α ≤ 0.07% for the marked tests.
entries.quote: The relative performance gains are all statistically signiﬁcant as indicated by ’*’ in table 3, with the signiﬁcance level α ≤0.07% for all tests.

entries.text: Using one and two context-dependent BDPF streams gives 42.16% and 34.42% WER, respectively.
entries.condition: Speaker-dependent audible BASE evaluation; the available PF stream is added in frequency order; active stream weights are distributed equally; 101-word vocabulary.
entries.quote: of 42.16%, and with two streams, the WER drops to 34.42%.

entries.text: Five streams achieve 31.25% WER, essentially the same as 31.49% with all nine streams.
entries.condition: Speaker-dependent audible BASE evaluation; equal weights across active context-dependent BDPF streams; 101-word vocabulary.

entries.text: Average Gaussian counts are 290 for the phoneme baseline, 1,690 for CI PFs and 2,489 for CD bundled PFs.
entries.condition: Systems in Table 2; per-stream means are 290, 169 and 248, respectively; PF training samples are reused across streams.
entries.quote:
Phoneme-based system
290
290

entries.text: A lattice of density 100 has 18.76% WER versus 31.49% for the system's first-best output.
entries.unit: lattice density; % lattice WER; % first-best WER
entries.condition: Speaker-dependent best context-dependent bundled-PF system; density means pruning retains 100 × reference-word-count nodes per utterance; audible BASE test, 101-word vocabulary.
entries.quote:
We achieve a lat-
tice WER of 18.76% compared to the 31.49% ﬁrst-best error rate of our
currently best system.

entries.text: The authors argue that bundling is what captures variability in PF representations: adding context without bundling raises WER, while context-dependent bundled PFs improve it.
entries.condition: Speaker-dependent comparison of context-dependent unbundled and bundled PF models.

entries.text: The incremental-stream experiment is presented as evidence that multiple bundled feature streams, rather than a single PF stream, are needed to obtain the full discrimination benefit.
entries.condition: Speaker-dependent context-dependent BDPF experiment; equal weights across available streams.

entries.text: The authors attribute BDPF gains partly to multi-stream reuse of training observations, with each sample contributing to the phoneme stream and each PF stream.
entries.unit: uses of each training sample in the nine-PF-stream system
entries.condition: Phoneme stream plus nine PF streams; the authors say this structure is crucial under the corpus's limited training-data constraint.

entries.text: The multi-speaker phoneme baseline achieves 62.15% WER averaged over 28 sessions from the 14 pilot speakers.
entries.condition: Audible pilot-study evaluation; pooled multi-speaker training and per-speaker/session test sets; the authors call the setup speaker-independent.
entries.quote: which for the multi-speaker scenario yields a WER of 62.15%, averaged over all 28 sessions of the 14 speakers.

entries.text: The multi-speaker models pool training data from all 14 pilot speakers and are then tested on the respective test sets for each of those speakers and sessions; speaker IDs therefore overlap train and test (inference from the stated protocol).
entries.condition: The paper labels this speaker-independent, but it does not describe a held-out-speaker test; the stated pooled training speakers are the evaluated speakers.
entries.quote: trained with the combined training data from the 14 speakers of the EMG-PIT pilot study

entries.text: Context-dependent phoneme modeling achieves 56.55% WER, a 9.01% relative gain over the 62.15% baseline.
entries.condition: Multi-speaker audible pilot evaluation; pooled training from 14 pilot speakers and evaluation across 28 sessions; CD phoneme models use 600 shared codebooks.
entries.quote: Consequently, the performance improved to 56.55% word error rate.

entries.text: Context-independent phonemes with context-dependent BDPF streams achieve 45.24% WER, with 20.19% relative gain as listed in Table 4.
entries.condition: Multi-speaker audible pilot evaluation; pooled 14-speaker training; nine context-dependent PF streams; trees use 220 leaves per stream.
entries.quote:
It can be seen that both systems which use context-dependent BDPFs
perform signiﬁcantly better than the context-dependent phoneme system.

entries.text: Context-dependent phonemes plus context-dependent BDPF streams achieve 44.95% WER; their 0.64% relative gain over the 45.24% system is not significant.
entries.condition: Multi-speaker audible pilot evaluation; pooled 14-speaker training; context-dependent BDPFs with a context-dependent phoneme stream.
entries.quote: The relative gain of 0.64% is not statistically signiﬁcant.

entries.text: Multi-speaker BDPF trees were grown to 220 leaves per feature stream, compared with 70 leaves in the speaker-dependent setup.
entries.condition: Nine PF streams; 220-leaf count experimentally selected for the larger pooled-training condition.
entries.quote: the BDPF clustering trees were grown to an experimentally determined optimal number of 220 leaf nodes

entries.text: The authors interpret the small, nonsignificant improvement from adding a context-dependent phoneme stream to BDPFs as evidence that the BDPFs already carry that context information.
entries.condition: Multi-speaker comparison of 45.24% versus 44.95% WER; difference reported as nonsignificant.

entries.text: The conclusion reports over 33% relative baseline WER reduction for speaker-dependent experiments and about 28% for the paper's speaker-independent/multi-speaker experiments; it describes 31.49% WER on the 101-word task as useful for silent-speech applications.
entries.unit: % relative reduction; % relative reduction; % WER; vocabulary words
entries.condition: Speaker-dependent result uses audible BASE tests; multi-speaker result uses the pilot-speaker pooled setup; the paper does not report a silent-speech test result.

entries.text: The paper presents EMG SSI as potentially resistant to ambient acoustic noise, private, and non-distracting because it senses articulation before speech becomes airborne.
entries.condition: This is an application motivation/claimed capability; the experiments reported here evaluate recognition accuracy on recorded, controlled-reading utterances, not field deployment.

entries.text: The authors say the approach can recognize silently mouthed speech because EMG depends on muscle activity rather than audible output.
entries.condition: Capability statement and corpus design; no silent-mode WER evaluation is reported in the results sections.

entries.text: The experiments use planned, phonetically balanced read speech rather than conversational or unplanned speech.
entries.condition: Controlled corpus collection; the authors selected read sentences to obtain phone coverage and avoid transcription work.

entries.text: The system does not use additional noise models because the authors handle planned speech.
entries.condition: PF multi-stream recognition experiments.

entries.text: The authors note that EMG varies with electrode position, temperature, humidity and tissue properties, favoring speaker- and often session-dependent systems.
entries.condition: The paper's main speaker-dependent experiment trains and tests within its per-speaker recording protocol; it does not establish robustness to electrode replacement or environmental changes.

entries.text: No random seeds, repeated-run protocol or run-to-run variance is reported for the recognition experiments.
entries.condition: Applies to speaker-dependent and multi-speaker results; the significance tests do not substitute for a reported seed/repetition protocol.
entries.quote: The relative performance gains are all statistically signiﬁcant as indicated by ’*’ in table 3, with the signiﬁcance level α ≤0.07% for all tests.

entries.text: The paper does not describe a separate validation set or nested selection procedure; it explicitly tunes speaker-dependent PF weights and bundling parameters on the test set.
entries.condition: The multi-speaker 220-leaf count is called experimentally optimal, but the data used to select it are not identified.
entries.quote: we optimized the parameters for the PF bundling on the test set.

entries.text: The normalization procedure behind the phrase ‘normalized mean’ is not specified; the fit/apply split for LDA and any per-session or per-channel scaling are also not described.
entries.condition: A normalized mean is mentioned in the TD15 formula, but the normalization formula and statistics are absent.

entries.text: No chance-level or shuffled-label reference performance is reported.
entries.condition: WER results are compared with phoneme and PF model baselines; no chance baseline is provided for the 101-word task.

entries.text: The exact LM training corpus partition, vocabulary coverage, word-penalty/LM-weight grid and selected final decoding parameters are not given.
entries.condition: The manuscript identifies a Broadcast News trigram and says decoding parameters are optimized by lattice rescoring; selection is not reported as nested on a held-out set.

entries.text: No independent check of acoustic forced-alignment quality or reference-transcription accuracy is reported.
entries.condition: Acoustic forced alignments initialize audible EMG phoneme training; the paper does not report manual alignment review or annotation agreement.

entries.text: The paper reports that Jou et al. (2007) found up to 10% relative WER improvement from adding PFs over a conventional phoneme-only EMG model.
entries.condition: Prior EMG recognition result cited by the target paper; the target text says this earlier system trained PF classifiers from phoneme middle frames.
entries.quote: using the PFs yields a relative WER improvement of up to 10% over the conventional phoneme-only model.

entries.text: The paper cites an earlier speaker-independent EMG triphone experiment reporting 11.5% relative improvement after training on about 77 minutes of EMG.
entries.unit: % relative improvement; minutes of EMG training
entries.condition: Prior result in Wand and Schultz (2009b); described as context-dependent phoneme modeling in a speaker-independent recognizer.

entries.text: The related-work section reports historical EMG recognition accuracy of 70% for a 10-word vocabulary, declining to 35% for 17 words.
entries.condition: Historical isolated-word EMG systems cited to Morse et al.; not results of the target experiments.

entries.text: The paper cites 93% average word accuracy for Chan et al.'s EMG recognition of English digits on a 10-word vocabulary.
entries.condition: Prior Chan et al. (2001) result, cited in the related-work section; not the target continuous-speech test.

entries.text: The authors say they previously demonstrated the first speech-recognition system handling seamless switches between audible and silent modes.
entries.condition: Prior demonstration cited by the target paper; the present paper does not evaluate seamless switching.

entries.text: The significance notation is inconsistent: Sec. 3.2 gives α = 0.7% (0.007) for the baseline/CI-PF test, while Table 3 later states α ≤ 0.07% for all tests.
entries.condition: The values differ by a factor of ten; the paper does not reconcile the two reports.
entries.quote: the signiﬁcance level α is at 0.7% (0.007).

entries.text: The conclusion characterizes the 31.49% average-WER result on the 101-word task as within useful range for silent-speech applications.
entries.condition: Conclusion claim; the reported evaluation used audible BASE sentences and does not itself score silent speech.
entries.quote: With this approach we achieved an average word error rate of 31.49% on a 101-word vocabulary task, bringing EMG-based speech recognition within useful range for silent speech applications.

entries.text: The related-work discussion reports 70% accuracy on a 10-word vocabulary for early EMG systems before describing the later decline to 35% on 17 words.
entries.condition: Historical isolated-word results cited to Morse et al.; not results of the target experiments.

entries.text: The paper cites an approximately 30% WER reduction from context-dependent phoneme modeling in conventional acoustic speech recognition.
entries.condition: General prior acoustic-ASR result cited as motivation for context-dependent PF modeling; not an EMG experiment in this paper.

entries.text: The pilot corpus phase contains 14 speakers, 28 sessions, 1,400 audible and 1,400 silent utterances, and 108 audible / 110 silent minutes.
entries.unit: speakers; sessions; utterances (audible / silent); minutes (audible / silent)
entries.condition: Pilot phase of EMG-PIT, Table 1; each pilot speaker participated in two sessions.

entries.text: The main corpus phase contains 64 speakers, 64 sessions, 3,200 audible and 3,200 silent utterances, and 287 audible / 251 silent minutes.
entries.unit: speakers; sessions; utterances (audible / silent); minutes (audible / silent)
entries.condition: Main phase of EMG-PIT, Table 1; one recording session per speaker.

entries.text: The acoustic recognizer used for forced alignment has a stated 10.2% WER on the clean F0 official Broadcast News test set.
entries.condition: Prior Broadcast News acoustic recognizer used to align audible EMG training utterances; this is not the target EMG test score.

entries.text: After acoustic initialization, the EMG phoneme models receive four iterations of Viterbi training.
entries.condition: Speaker-dependent baseline training procedure; the paper does not report random seeds or repetitions.

entries.text: The conclusion reports about 28% relative baseline WER reduction for its speaker-independent (multi-speaker) system.
entries.condition: Multi-speaker results use pooled training data from all 14 pilot speakers and evaluation on their sessions; no held-out speaker group is described.
entries.quote:
and by about 28% in the speaker-
independent system.

entries.text: The authors emphasize that dependencies among PFs are learned algorithmically from data, rather than supplied as hand-written rules or educated guesses.
entries.condition: Data-driven decision-tree bundling for EMG PF streams.

entries.text: The recognizer uses HMM acoustic models with fully continuous GMMs and phoneme-based models; whether the phoneme stream is context-independent or context-dependent is not specified in Sec. 3.2.
entries.condition: BDPFs used for final training and decoding

entries.text: Yes. PF acoustic models for feature substates are combined with the conventional phoneme recognizer in a multi-stream system; dependent PFs are bundled by standard decision-tree clustering.
entries.condition: All experiments use bundled phonetic features

entries.text: Sec. 3.2 describes a weighted sum of streams but does not state how stream weights were selected or which data were used to choose them.
entries.condition: Checked Sec. 3.2

entries.text: The study uses 14 pilot speakers with two sessions each plus speaker 15 with one additional session; BASE sentences are test and SPEC sentences training, so there is no held-out-speaker test. MLLR adaptation is not stated in Secs. 3–4.
entries.condition: Speaker-specific train/test split; checked Secs. 3–4 for MLLR

entries.text: The standard per-speaker test has 10 sentences and a 108-word vocabulary with a trigram BN LM; audible and silently mouthed speech are tested. Speaker 15's separate experiment has 60 test sentences per mode.
entries.condition: 108-word vocabulary; trigram BN language model; audible and silent/voicelessly mouthed EMG
entries.quote: This resulted in a test set of 10 sentences per speaker with a vocabulary of 108 words.

entries.text: Best silent-EMG result is 30.10% WER for experienced speaker 15; the paper says this is about the same as that speaker's audible result, but gives no exact speaker-15 audible baseline. The recognizer's average audible WER is 30.19%.
entries.condition: Silent EMG, speaker 15; Cross-Modal Labeling generally gives the best results; exact same-speaker audible comparison not reported
entries.quote:
for speaker 15, who is the one speaker who had recorded several
silent speech sessions before, the best WER achieved on silent
EMG is 30.10%

entries.text: Secs. 3–4 do not describe a separate development set or an explicit test-set tuning protocol; TD15 was carried over from audible-EMG baseline experiments.
entries.condition: Checked Secs. 3–4

entries.text: The system uses first-order HMMs with GMMs and tests word, syllable and phoneme units; it evaluates CI models, CD triphones and clustered (CL) phoneme models, with context clustering for CD models.
entries.value: First-order HMM/GMM; words, syllables, phonemes; CI, CD triphones, CL
entries.condition: Three states per phoneme/model unit
entries.quote: First order HMMs with Gaussian mixture models are used as

entries.text: Secs. 4.3–5 describe word, syllable and phoneme HMM units, but do not report PF/AF classifiers combined as streams, PF bundling/clustering, or stream-weight selection.
entries.condition: Checked Secs. 4.3–5

entries.text: Two subjects recorded five sessions each; the same speakers contribute to training and testing because recordings of each word are split into train/test sets and swapped. No held-out-speaker test is described, and MLLR adaptation is not stated in Secs. 4–5.
entries.condition: Within-speaker recording split; checked Secs. 4–5 for MLLR

entries.text: The corpus has 32 English expressions built from 21 syllables; each session records 20 non-audible repetitions per word and testing uses half the recordings per fold. Recognition is on silent/non-audible speech; a language model is not specified in Secs. 4–5.
entries.condition: Two-fold round-robin seen-word test and disjoint-vocabulary unseen-word test; non-audible speech

entries.text: Secs. 4.5–5 do not state a language model or LM type for decoding.
entries.condition: Checked Secs. 4.5–5

entries.text: Best seen-word accuracy is 82.9% for word models in round-robin testing; on unseen words, clustered phonemes reach 62.4%, versus 58.8% for CD phonemes and 55.1% for CD syllables. These are accuracies, not WERs.
entries.condition: 82.9%: seen words, word models; 62.4%: unseen words, clustered phoneme models; unseen-word comparators: CD phonemes 58.8%, CD syllables 55.1%

entries.text: Feature settings were selected from round-robin test results: 27-ms windows plus TDC performed best and were reused in subsequent experiments. No separate development set is described in Secs. 5.1–5.2.
entries.condition: Chosen after round-robin evaluation
entries.quote: Since the systems with a window size of 27 ms and usage of the TDC feature performed best, these features were used in all following experiments.

entries.text: The recognizer uses phoneme-based, context-independent acoustic models; Sec. 2.3 does not specify the EMG model's HMM topology/type or GMM configuration.
entries.value: Context-independent phoneme models; HMM/GMM details not specified
entries.condition: Checked Secs. 2.3–3

entries.text: Secs. 2.3–4 describe phoneme-based acoustic models and EMG feature extraction, but do not report PF/AF classifiers combined as streams, PF bundling, or stream-weight selection.
entries.condition: Checked Secs. 2.3–4

entries.text: Data come from one male speaker and one session, with 380 training and 120 test utterances from that speaker; no speaker-held-out test is possible. MLLR adaptation is not stated in Secs. 2–4.
entries.condition: Same speaker in train and test; checked Secs. 2–4 for MLLR

entries.text: There are 120 news-article test utterances, a 108-word decoding vocabulary, and a trigram BN LM; the tested mode is normal audible speech, not silent/mouthed speech.
entries.condition: Trigram BN LM; audible speech

entries.text: The best EMG-feature result is 32.0% WER with E4 features and a 50-ms delay, compared with 86.8% for the plain spectral-feature baseline.
entries.condition: E4, 50-ms EMG delay; baseline: plain spectral features at 86.8% WER

entries.text: No separate development set is described in Secs. 2–5; delays from 0–90 ms and feature configurations are compared by WER, and 50 ms is then used in later experiments. The paper does not explicitly identify a held-out dev set for this selection.
entries.condition: Delay selected from reported WER experiments; checked Secs. 2–5
entries.quote: Therefore, we report results for the remainder of experiments at 50 ms delay.

entries.text: The initial EMG recognizer is HMM-based with fully continuous GMMs and context-independent phoneme states; the paper also evaluates generalized CD triphones clustered with a decision tree into 600 models.
entries.value: HMM/fully continuous GMM; CI phonemes; CD generalized triphones, 600 clustered models
entries.condition: Initial CI system and later context-dependent experiment

entries.text: Secs. 3–4 describe E4/wavelet features and phone HMMs, but no PF/AF classifiers, multi-stream feature combination, PF bundling, or stream weights are reported for this paper's experiments.
entries.condition: Checked Secs. 3–4.5

entries.text: The corpus has 13 speakers with two sessions each plus speaker 14 with one session; cross-speaker training excludes both sessions of the test speaker, and adaptation applies MLLR using one session of that speaker.
entries.condition: Cross-speaker test; speaker-held-out training; MLLR adaptation condition
entries.quote: We performed speaker adaptive training by initially training acoustic models based on the training data of all speakers but the two sessions of the test speaker.

entries.text: For the 13-speaker corpus, test sets have 10 sentences per speaker/session, a 101-word decoding vocabulary and a trigram BN LM (perplexity 24.24); results use audible utterances only. The added speaker-14 legacy test has 120 sentences.
entries.condition: 101-word vocabulary; trigram BN LM; audible speech only

entries.text: The reported speaker-dependent E4 average is 57.27% WER; the paper's context-dependent result is 60.97%, improving on its 68.92% context-independent baseline by 11.5% relative.
entries.condition: 57.27%: speaker-dependent E4; 60.97% CD vs 68.92% CI baseline: 11.5% relative improvement
entries.quote: The overall average performance of the context-independent system has a WER of 68.92%, which by context-dependent modeling drops to 60.97%.

questions.q: Do the reported results demonstrate recognition of silent speech?
questions.answer: No silent-mode WER is reported. The scored experiments use audible BASE test utterances from the pilot subset, despite the corpus containing both audible and mouthed-silent recordings.

questions.q: Were stream weights and PF-bundling settings selected on an independent validation set?
questions.answer: No independent validation set is described. The authors state that PF stream weights and speaker-dependent bundling parameters were optimized on the test set; the selection data for the multi-speaker leaf count are not identified.

questions.q: Does the multi-speaker experiment test generalization to unseen speakers?
questions.answer: The stated protocol pools training data from all 14 pilot speakers and tests those speakers' sessions. It therefore does not establish performance on a held-out speaker population (inference).

questions.q: What is the strongest reported result and its evaluation condition?
questions.answer: The best speaker-dependent first-best result is 31.49% average WER for context-dependent bundled PFs on audible BASE tests from 14 pilot speakers (28 sessions), using a 101-word vocabulary; best/worst speaker WERs are about 10%/50%. A lattice at density 100 scores 18.76% WER.
